h1: Rose, hibiscus and other flowers in beer without a soapy finish
title: Rose and Hibiscus in Beer, Done Right | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew with rose, hibiscus, butterfly pea and other flowers without soapy or perfumed flavours: sourcing, timing, dosing and colour.
teaser: A little rose tastes like a garden. A little too much tastes like a bar of soap. Here is how brewers stay on the right side of that line.
standfirst: Flowers are a natural fit for Indian craft beer: rose, hibiscus, jasmine and butterfly pea are all familiar from food and drink here. They are also easy to overdo. This guide covers sourcing, timing and dosing so floral beers taste deliberate.
sections:
Most floral aromas come from terpene alcohols such as geraniol, linalool and citronellol. Hops contain many of the same compounds, which is why some hops smell of rose or lavender.

At low levels these read as fresh and floral. At higher levels the brain files them under cosmetics and soap. The window between pleasant and perfumed is narrow. It shifts with carbonation, sweetness and the base beer. A dry, highly carbonated beer shows floral notes more strongly than a sweeter, fuller one.

Flowers from the florist or temple market are grown for looks, not for eating. They are often sprayed heavily. Do not use them.

Buy dried flowers sold as food ingredients: dried rose petals and buds for tea or cooking, dried hibiscus (the roselle calyces sold for tea), dried butterfly pea flowers and food-grade chamomile. Ask for the supplier's food safety licence details and a batch number. For commercial brewing, keep these with your ingredient records.

Rose water is another option. Check that it is a food-grade product made for cooking, not a cosmetic toner. It should contain no preservatives you would not want in beer. Strength varies a lot between brands.

Dried flowers carry microbes, so they need either heat or alcohol to be safe.

  • Whirlpool. Add to the whirlpool once wort has cooled to around 75 to 80 °C, for 10 to 20 minutes. This sanitises the flowers and extracts colour and flavour without boiling off the delicate aroma.
  • Post-fermentation. Add as a sanitised tea or tincture to the conditioning tank. This keeps the most aroma, since nothing is driven off by fermentation CO2.
  • Avoid the full boil. Boiling drives off aroma and can extract bitter, tea-like tannins.

Many brewers split the addition: a whirlpool charge for colour and body, then a measured post-fermentation dose for aroma.

• Rose. The most likely to turn soapy. Pairs well with wheat beers, light lagers and saisons. Desi gulab varieties are intensely fragrant, so dose lightly.
  • Hibiscus. Brings tartness and a vivid red to pink colour from anthocyanins. It is less soapy and more like cranberry or sour cherry. Excellent in wheat beers, goses and light sours.
  • Butterfly pea. Little flavour, but a striking blue that turns purple or pink as pH falls. In most finished beer, which sits around pH 4, expect purple rather than blue.
  • Jasmine. Heady and sweet, best in tiny amounts with a pale lager or a green tea beer.
  • Chamomile. Honeyed and gentle, easy to use in a witbier.
  • Lavender. Very easy to overdo. Most brewers find it soapy above the faintest trace.

Our guides to brewing with Indian spices and adding fruit to beer cover similar timing questions.

Make a concentrated tea or tincture of known strength: for example, 10 g dried petals steeped in 100 ml of just-boiled water for ten minutes, then strained. Add measured amounts to 100 ml samples of finished beer with a pipette and taste blind with a small panel. Choose the level where the flower is clear but not perfumed, then scale to tank volume.

Taste again after two weeks in package. Floral aroma fades over time while colour stays, so a beer that tasted slightly strong on packaging day may be right a fortnight later. Write that into your release schedule.
Pairing flowers with the base beer

The base beer decides how much floral character it can carry. A light wheat beer or a saison gives flowers a soft, slightly spicy frame. A crisp pilsner leaves nowhere to hide, so even a small dose of rose stands out. A sour or a gose works well with hibiscus because the acidity matches the flower's own tartness.

Bitter, resinous hops often clash with rose and jasmine. If the flower is the point of the beer, keep bitterness low and choose hops with soft floral or citrus notes that support it. Our guide to beer aroma vocabulary helps a tasting panel describe what they find.

Anthocyanins in hibiscus and rose are sensitive to pH, oxygen and light. Colour can drift from bright red towards brown over weeks, especially if the beer sits warm. Keep floral beers cold, packaged with low oxygen and in cans or brown bottles.

Petal fragments add haze and sediment. Use a fine mesh bag and allow time for settling or crash cooling before packaging. Record supplier, lot, dose and timing for every batch, because dried flower strength varies from one harvest to the next.
faqs: How do I stop rose beer tasting of soap?
Dose lower than you think, using a bench trial with a measured rose tea or tincture. Add most of the rose after fermentation, where you can control it.
When should I add hibiscus to beer?
In the whirlpool at around 75 to 80 °C or as a sanitised tea after fermentation. It adds tartness and a strong red colour.
Why did my butterfly pea beer turn purple?
Butterfly pea colour changes with pH. Most beer is acidic enough to turn it purple or pink rather than blue.
